text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on March 20 in history.
43 B.C. - Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Roman poet, born. He was exiled from Rome in 9 A.D.
1413 - King Henry IV of England, the first king of the House of Lancaster, died. He had ruled since 1399.
1549 - Sir Thomas Seymour, Lord High Admiral of England and husband of Henry VIII's widow Catherine Parr, died.
1602 - The Dutch East India Company was established. During its 96-year history it became one of the world's most powerful companies.
1727 - Sir Isaac Newton, British scientist and mathematician, died. He was noted for his theories and discoveries especially that of gravity.
1815 - Napoleon arrived back in Paris from Elba to reclaim power at the start of "The Hundred Days" before defeat at Waterloo.
1828 - Henrik Ibsen, Norwegian poet and playwright, born. His realistic social dramas, including "A Doll's House" and "Hedda Gabler" influenced many writers.
1852 - Harriet Beecher Stowe's anti-slavery novel "Uncle Tom's Cabin", was first published in book form.
1890 - Beniamino Gigli, Italian operatic tenor, born; with a repertory of over 60 roles, he retired in 1955 after over 40 years singing.
1890 - Lauritz Melchior, Danish operatic tenor, born. Probably the greatest Wagnerian tenor of all time, he sang Wagner's "Tristan und Isolde" over 200 times.
1894 - Lajos Kossuth, Hungarian patriot who was the inspiration behind Hungary's drive for independence from Austria, died.
1908 - Sir Michael Redgrave, English actor, born. Best known for his roles in "The Captive Heart" and "The Browning Version".
1917 - Dame Vera Lynn, English singer and sweetheart of British forces during World War Two, born.
1920 - The first flight between England and South Africa was completed by H.A. van Rejneveld and C.J. Brand.
1928 - Ferdinand Foch, Marshal of France and commander of Allied forces during the closing months of World War One, died aged 77.
1933 - The first concentration camp was opened in Germany, at Dachau.
1934 - The first practical tests of radar were carried out at Kiel Harbour, Germany, by Dr Rudolph Kuenhold.
1939 - Brian Mulroney, Canadian statesman, born; as prime minister, he initiated a free trade agreement with the United States.
1945 - George Nathaniel Curzon, Viceroy of India, died. Viceroy from 1899-1905 nd and then foreign secretary from 1919-24.
1945 - Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, editor and poet, died. His close association with Oscar Wilde eventually led to Wilde's trial and imprisonment for homosexual practices.
1948 - Eugene Ormandy conducted the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra on CBS TV in the first symphony concert to be televised in the United States.
1956 - Full independence of Tunisia was granted under a protocol signed with France.
1964 - Brendan Behan, Irish writer and playwright, died. A member of the IRA, he was imprisoned twice.
1974 - An attempt was made to kidnap Princess Anne in The Mall, London.
1976 - Patricia Hearst, after an eight-week trial, was found guilty of armed robbery in April 1974 in the United States.
1980 - Lord Soames announced the end of martial law in Rhodesia.
1984 - The Lebanese conference in Lausanne on national reconciliation ended without agreement on fundamental political reforms.
1993 - In England, two IRA bombs in litter bins exploded in a shopping centre in the town of Warrington, killing two boys.
1995 - Up to 35,000 Turkish troops launched an attack across the border with Iraq in pursuit of separatist Kurdish rebels.
1996 - One of Iraq's top Gulf War generals, Staff-Lieutenant General Nazar Khazraji, defected to Jordan.
1996 - British government said for the first time that mad cow disease could probably be transmitted to humans.
